name: Light Green-Yellow
lede: Light Green-Yellow is a pale, bright yellow-green from Ridgway's 1912 atlas, filed again by name in the 1955 ISCC-NBS dictionary, close enough on screen to its sibling Light Chalcedony Yellow to be mistaken for it.

sections.title: A Ridgway tone with a near-twin
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* carries this swatch on plate V, hue 27, tone d [1]. The 1955 ISCC-NBS dictionary files the exact name "Light Green-Yellow" under block 101, "light greenish yellow" [2]. The name builds "light" onto [[green-yellow]], a straightforward hue-pair compound rather than a word drawn from nature or trade [1].

In our color library its closest neighbors are [[pale-butter]] and [[dark-cream]], both about 2.9 units away, nearly the same color on screen [3]. [[light-chalcedony-yellow]] sits 3.3 units off and duller, despite sharing the same block in the 1955 dictionary [2][3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive of 23,781 paintings matches this tone in 38 of them, about 0.16 percent, as photographed, rarer than 58 percent of the named colors we track [4]. It peaks in the 1500s, present in 5 of the 2,231 paintings from that century, 1.5 times the rate its museums' own baseline would predict [4].

Inside a painting it most often plays an accent, in 64 percent of its 28 clearly-ranked appearances [4]. The earliest dated match is 1490, in a painting by Lorenzo Costa, 422 years before the name's first 1912 record, so this is a look-alike hue in an old photograph, not proof of the name's age [4]. The archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and the match is a computed color reading, not a pigment identification [4].
